description: Continuous, fartlek, interval, circuit, weight and plyometric training and their effects on fitness.
content_html:
Choosing the Right Training Method

Not all training is the same. A marathon runner who only lifts heavy weights will not improve aerobic endurance; a sprinter who only plods along at a slow jog will never develop the explosive power needed off the blocks. The principle of specificity demands that the training method matches the demands of the sport. This lesson covers six key methods: continuous, fartlek, interval, circuit, weight/resistance and plyometric training, plus fitness classes such as body pump, aerobics, Pilates and yoga.

Continuous Training

Continuous training involves exercising at a constant pace for at least 20 minutes without rest breaks. Running, cycling, swimming and rowing are all used. The heart rate is maintained within the aerobic training zone (60–80% of maximum heart rate). Cardiovascular endurance is the primary component developed. Advantages: simple, cheap and easy to monitor. Disadvantages: can be monotonous, does not develop anaerobic capacity, and is less suitable for sports requiring explosive bursts of speed.

Fartlek Training

Fartlek training (Swedish for “speed play”) mixes continuous aerobic effort with bursts of higher-intensity work. The athlete varies pace and terrain spontaneously — for example, sprinting between lampposts, then jogging until recovered, then climbing a hill at pace. Because it crosses both aerobic and anaerobic zones, fartlek develops both cardiovascular endurance and speed/power. It is particularly well suited to games players (e.g. football, rugby) who work at varying intensities throughout a match. Advantages: varied and engaging, replicates the unpredictable nature of games. Disadvantages: intensity is harder to measure precisely, which makes it difficult to monitor overload.

Interval Training

Interval training alternates periods of high-intensity effort with rest or active recovery. The work-to-rest ratio can be adjusted to target different energy systems and fitness components. Short, very intense intervals (e.g. 10–30 seconds at near-maximum effort, long rest) develop anaerobic capacity and speed. Longer intervals (e.g. 3–5 minutes at 80–85% max HR, shorter rest) develop cardiovascular endurance and muscular endurance. HIIT (high-intensity interval training) is a popular form using very short maximal efforts (20–40 seconds) with equally short rest, placing high demands on both energy systems. Advantages: very time-efficient, versatile, effective for aerobic and anaerobic development. Disadvantages: physically demanding, higher injury risk if not progressed carefully.

Key Fact

Primary fitness components by method: continuous → cardiovascular endurance; fartlek → cardiovascular endurance + speed; interval → cardiovascular endurance, muscular endurance or speed/anaerobic capacity (depending on ratios); circuit → muscular endurance + cardiovascular endurance; weight/resistance → strength or muscular endurance; plyometric → power.

Circuit Training

Circuit training involves moving through a series of exercise stations in sequence, performing a set number of repetitions or working for a set time at each station before moving on. A typical circuit might include press-ups, sit-ups, squat jumps, star jumps, dumbbell curls and shuttle runs. Because minimal rest occurs between stations and the circuit covers whole-body movements, both muscular endurance and cardiovascular endurance are developed. Circuit training is highly adaptable: adding resistance increases the strength component; increasing pace and reducing rest raises the cardiovascular demand. Advantages: can be tailored to any component of fitness, requires little specialist equipment, suitable for groups. Disadvantages: technique can deteriorate under fatigue.

Weight and Resistance Training

Weight training (also called resistance training) uses external resistance — free weights, resistance machines or bodyweight — to overload the muscular system. The fitness component developed depends on the weight and repetition scheme used. Heavy loads with low repetitions (1–6 reps, >85% of one rep max) develop maximal strength. Moderate loads with moderate repetitions (8–12 reps, 65–80% of one rep max) develop muscle hypertrophy. Light loads with high repetitions (15+ reps, below 65% of one rep max) develop muscular endurance. One rep max (1RM) is the maximum weight that can be lifted once with correct form. Training intensity in resistance work is expressed as a percentage of 1RM. Advantages: highly targeted, progressive load is easy to measure. Disadvantages: requires equipment, risk of injury without correct technique.

Plyometric Training

Plyometric training uses rapid, explosive movements to develop power. Activities include jump squats, bounding, box jumps and depth jumps (stepping off a box and immediately jumping upward). The key mechanism is the stretch-shortening cycle: the muscle is rapidly stretched (eccentric contraction) just before it contracts explosively (concentric contraction). This pre-stretching stores elastic energy that is released during the explosive phase, producing greater power than a concentric contraction alone. Plyometrics are particularly useful for sprinters, jumpers, basketball and volleyball players. Advantages: directly develops sport-specific explosive power. Disadvantages: high impact, requires good base strength to avoid injury, especially in the knees and ankles.

Key Fact

Advantages and disadvantages: continuous is simple but monotonous; fartlek is engaging but hard to measure intensity; interval is versatile but carries higher injury risk; circuit is adaptable but technique can suffer under fatigue; weight training is targeted but needs equipment; plyometrics develops sport-specific power but is high impact.

Several fitness class formats are part of the specification. Body pump is a barbell-based class using light to moderate weights with high repetitions, primarily developing muscular endurance. Aerobics classes (also called step aerobics or dance fitness) use continuous rhythmic movement to develop cardiovascular endurance. Pilates focuses on core strength, postural alignment and controlled movement, primarily developing strength and flexibility of the trunk. Yoga combines static poses, controlled breathing and stretching, primarily developing flexibility and balance. These class formats can complement sport-specific training — a footballer might use yoga to improve hip flexibility and Pilates to strengthen core stability.

When an exam question asks you to evaluate a training method for a specific sport, follow this structure: (1) name the component of fitness the method develops; (2) explain why that component is important in the sport; (3) identify a key advantage of the method; (4) identify a key disadvantage or limitation. For a 4-mark Discuss question on interval training for a games player, you might write: interval training develops both aerobic and anaerobic capacity (relevant to football where intensity varies continuously); it can be structured to replicate the high-intensity bursts of a match; however, it is demanding and injury risk is higher than continuous training if rest periods are too short.
exam_tip_html: A common error on training methods questions is stating a method without linking it to the specific fitness component or sport. “Circuit training is good for athletes” earns nothing; “circuit training develops muscular endurance and cardiovascular endurance, which are essential for a basketball player sustaining repeated explosive efforts across four quarters” earns full marks. For Discuss questions (4 marks), always present both advantages and disadvantages — mark schemes award half marks for one-sided answers. For Assess or Evaluate questions (6–9 marks), rank the methods and justify which is most appropriate for the given athlete or sport, using specific fitness component links and sporting examples throughout.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Six key methods: continuous (cardiovascular endurance); fartlek (cardiovascular endurance + speed); interval/HIIT (cardiovascular endurance, muscular endurance or anaerobic power depending on ratios); circuit (muscular endurance + cardiovascular endurance); weight/resistance (strength or muscular endurance); plyometric (power).
  • Each method has advantages and disadvantages — exam questions require both sides. Choice of method must be justified by linking to the relevant fitness component and the demands of the sport.
  • One rep max (1RM) is the benchmark for resistance training intensity: heavy/low reps → strength; moderate/moderate reps → hypertrophy; light/high reps → muscular endurance.

practice_questions.text:
Which training method involves alternating faster and slower effort periods over varied terrain without fixed rest intervals?
A) Continuous training
B) Circuit training
C) Fartlek training
D) Weight training

practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for describing explosive/rapid movement; 1 mark for reference to the stretch-shortening cycle or the aim of developing power. Full definition: training that uses rapid explosive movements exploiting the stretch-shortening cycle of muscles to develop power.

practice_questions.text: Describe one advantage and one disadvantage of using interval training to prepare a 16-year-old middle-distance runner for competition.
practice_questions.marks: Advantage (up to 2 marks): interval training allows the runner to work at a higher intensity than continuous training by including recovery periods (1); this develops both cardiovascular endurance and anaerobic capacity needed for the finishing kick in a race (1). Disadvantage (up to 2 marks): interval training is physically demanding and the risk of injury increases if recovery periods are too short (1); it requires careful monitoring to ensure the correct work-to-rest ratio for the runner's current fitness level (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how weight training can be adapted to develop either muscular strength or muscular endurance, using specific examples of how the load and repetitions would differ.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: for muscular strength, the athlete uses a heavy load (above 85% of 1RM) with low repetitions (1-6 reps) so the muscle is maximally overloaded in each set (1); for muscular endurance, a light load (below 65% of 1RM) with high repetitions (15+) keeps the muscle working under fatigue for an extended period (1).

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old county-level rugby player wants to improve her fitness over a 12-week pre-season block. Analyse which training methods would be most suitable for her sport and explain how they would be combined in a programme.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Fartlek training develops both aerobic base and speed, replicating the variable intensity of a rugby match (phases of sustained effort followed by sprints). Interval/HIIT develops anaerobic capacity needed for explosive tackles, scrums and sprints. Circuit training builds muscular endurance across whole-body movements relevant to rugby. Plyometrics develop the explosive power needed for jumping in lineouts or accelerating from stationary. A combined programme (e.g. fartlek twice weekly, circuit once, plyometrics once, with rest days) applies progressive overload by increasing intensity and duration week by week. Technically precise, consistent rugby application.

Secure: Identifies and justifies two or three methods with rugby application. Addresses combination.

Developing: Names methods without full application. Some connection to rugby.

Emerging: Names one method. No combination addressed.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate whether plyometric training or continuous training would be more beneficial for a club-level 100m sprinter. Use the principles of training to support your judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: For plyometrics — develops power through the stretch-shortening cycle; directly relevant to the explosive start and acceleration phase of a 100m race; satisfies specificity (explosive power is the primary demand). For continuous training — develops cardiovascular endurance, which helps with recovery between training sessions and warm-down; however, a 100m race is approximately 10 seconds and predominantly anaerobic, so cardiovascular endurance is not the limiting factor in race performance. Conclusion: plyometric training is more directly beneficial to the sprinter's event-specific performance; continuous training plays a supportive role in general conditioning but should not dominate the programme. References overtraining (mixing methods avoids repetitive strain), progressive overload (plyometric load increases across the programme). Balanced, applies principles, firm conclusion.

Secure: Argues both methods with sprinting application. Principles referenced. Reaches conclusion.

Developing: Focuses more on one method. Some sporting application.

Emerging: Describes one method. No evaluation.

knowledge_checks.q: Which training method primarily develops power by exploiting the stretch-shortening cycle?
To develop muscular strength using weight training, an athlete uses a _____ load with a low number of repetitions.
_____ training involves moving through a series of exercise stations in sequence with minimal rest, developing muscular endurance and cardiovascular endurance.
Match each training method to its primary fitness component:

flashcard_questions.q: What component of fitness does continuous training primarily develop?

flashcard_questions.a: Cardiovascular endurance and speed, by mixing intensities across varied terrain.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key advantage of interval training over continuous training?
flashcard_questions.a: It allows higher intensities to be reached by including planned recovery periods.

flashcard_questions.q: What fitness component does plyometric training develop?

flashcard_questions.a: The maximum weight an athlete can lift once with correct form.

flashcard_questions.q: What load and rep range develops muscular endurance in weight training?
flashcard_questions.a: Light load (below 65% of 1RM) with 15 or more repetitions.
High-intensity interval training: short maximal bursts alternating with short rest periods.

flashcard_questions.q: What fitness component does circuit training mainly develop?
What fitness class primarily develops cardiovascular endurance through continuous rhythmic movement?
What fitness class focuses on core strength, posture and controlled movement?
What sport is fartlek training especially well suited to, and why?
flashcard_questions.a: Games sports (e.g. football), because it replicates variable-intensity match demands.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the stretch-shortening cycle in plyometric training?
flashcard_questions.a: Rapid eccentric stretch followed by explosive concentric contraction, releasing stored elastic energy.

glossary_terms.definition: Sustained exercise at a steady pace without rest periods, lasting at least 20 minutes, primarily developing cardiovascular endurance.
A form of continuous training that mixes intensities, alternating faster and slower effort periods over varied terrain without fixed rest intervals.
Training that alternates periods of high-intensity effort with planned rest or low-intensity recovery periods, allowing the body to work at higher intensities than continuous training permits.
High-intensity interval training: alternating short maximal-effort bursts with very short rest periods, placing high demands on both aerobic and anaerobic systems.
A training method in which a series of exercises (stations) are completed in sequence with minimal rest between stations, targeting multiple muscle groups.
Training using free weights, machines or bodyweight to develop strength or muscular endurance, depending on load and repetition scheme.
The maximum weight an athlete can lift in a single repetition of an exercise with correct form.
Training that uses explosive movements exploiting the stretch-shortening cycle of muscles to develop power, such as jump squats, bounding and depth jumps.
